clues.title: Plate: white with blue top stripe, red commercial
text: Licence plates in Brazil were **white **until 2018. Now, a **white plate with a blue stripe** on top is used. Red is still used for commercial vehicles.

images.caption: Brazilian plates: standard, standard from 2018 and red commercial

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Plates were white until 2018. Now they are white with a blue stripe on top. Commercial vehicles still use red plates.

clues.title: Language: Portuguese (-ão, lh, nh)
text: **Portuguese **is spoken in Brazil, as opposed to most Latin American countries which speak Spanish. Compared to Spanish, some essential differences are that Portuguese uses -ão rather than -ón, -ch/-lh instead of -ll and -nh instead of -ñ.

images.caption: Portuguese text with the characters ã, o and ç shown large

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Portuguese, not Spanish. Look for -ão instead of -ón, lh/ch instead of ll, and nh instead of ñ.

clues.title: Landscape: red soil
text: Soil in most of Brazil is distinctly **red**. It can range from a [light pink](https://goo.gl/maps/n8fe3fywheFqKCTPA) around Mato Grosso to a deep maroon near the Paraná river. The soil is usually not red in the North East, or in the majority of Rio Grande do Sul, however.
NOTE: Parts of Paraguay and the nearby Argentine province of Misiones have deep red soil, as well a handful of other regions around the world.

images.caption: Two photos: a red dirt plot beside a road with a pond, and red soil with tall grass

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Soil in most of Brazil is distinctly red, from light pink around Mato Grosso to deep maroon near the Paraná river. Usually not red in the Northeast or most of Rio Grande do Sul. Paraguay and Misiones (Argentina) have deep red soil too.

clues.title: Pole: ladder-like rectangular concrete
text: The most common poles in Brazil have some resemblance to a **ladder **in the bottom portion. They are rectangular, have long segments running through the bottom, and small holes near the top.
NOTE: Paraguay uses similar poles.

images.caption: Rectangular concrete poles, one with a white-painted base; the red arrow points at the second pole

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The most common poles are rectangular with long segments running through the bottom like a ladder, and small holes near the top. Paraguay uses similar poles.

clues.title: Sign: backs of road signs painted black
text: Most Brazilian road signs have the backs painted **black**.
NOTE: This is also common in Paraguay.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most road signs have their backs painted black. Also common in Paraguay.

clues.title: Route marker: blue with road number and km
text: **Blue road markers** with the road number and kilometre can be seen on the sides of roads.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Blue markers show the road number and kilometre. The first two letters of a state road number are the state code (SP, MG...), except roads starting BR.

clues.title: Chevron: yellow arrows on black
text: Brazil uses **yellow **on **black **chevrons, as opposed to most of South America, which use black on yellow chevrons.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Chevrons are yellow on black, the opposite of most of South America (black on yellow).

clues.title: Road lines: double yellow centre, white edges
text: Roads in Brazil will usually feature **double yellow** middle lines, with white outer lines. Roads can occasionally have a [single dashed yellow line](https://goo.gl/maps/c8XDntyn1zgp9gah9).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Double yellow centre lines with white edge lines. Narrow roads sometimes have a single dashed yellow line.

clues.title: Road: white painted kerbs
text: There are frequently **white painted kerbs** on Brazilian roads.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: White painted kerbs are common on roads.

clues.title: Houses: orange tiled roofs
text: Many houses throughout Brazil have **orange tiled roofs**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Many houses have orange tiled roofs.

clues.title: Satellite dish: transparent
text: It is fairly common to see **transparent satellite dishes**, which within Latin America is generally unique to Brazil.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Transparent satellite dishes are fairly common and generally unique to this country in Latin America.

clues.title: Houses: blue water tanks on roofs
text: **Blue Fortlev water tanks **are often seen on Brazilian roofs.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Blue water tanks (Fortlev) often sit on roofs.

clues.title: Google car: white, coiled stubby antenna (Gen 3)
text: In Generation 3 coverage, you can see two different cars:
- A white car with a [**stubby antenna**](https://goo.gl/maps/NhuDAxCVQ9TjhSUF7). There is a diagonal coil wrapped around the antenna.
- A white car with [**no antenna**](https://goo.gl/maps/nKHjWrdrmbWcUULn6).
The car’s colour is not always visible, meaning you will often see either just the stubby antenna, or no hints of the car at all.
The stubby antenna with a diagonal coil can also be found in Ecuador, Colombia, and Mexico.

images.caption: A coiled stubby antenna on the white car blur at the centre

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In older Gen 3 coverage (blurrier, softer colours): a white car with a stubby antenna wrapped in a diagonal coil, or a white car with no antenna, often with no car visible at all. The coiled antenna also appears in Ecuador, Colombia and Mexico.

clues.title: Google car: blue, white with blue stripe, or white
text: The Generation 4 cars you can find in Brazil have a visible front, and have one of the following three colour patterns:
- [**Blue**](https://goo.gl/maps/cX9hiLoFAWmSxYLp8)
- [**White with a blue stripe**](https://goo.gl/maps/8m72fEE5hMYAQKF27)
- [**White**](https://goo.gl/maps/fkcFJmPtRwACz2Jv7)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Newer Gen 4 cars show the front and come in three looks: blue, white with a blue stripe, or plain white.

clues.title: Google car: low small camera, big round blur
text: Brazil also has Generation 4 “smallcam” coverage, which is mounted lower than regular Generation 4 and has a relatively big circular blur with a small protrusion at the front.
NOTE: Brazil, Peru and Argentina are the only South American countries with smallcam.

images.caption: Four panels labelled front panned down, front panned straight, back panned down and good blur (front)

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Some Gen 4 coverage uses a camera mounted lower, with a big round blur and a small bump at the front. Only Brazil, Peru and Argentina have it in South America.

clues.title: Coverage: mostly the eastern half
text: Most of the coverage in Brazil is along the **eastern **half, with only sparse coverage in the Amazon.

It is useful for beginning players to start forming a rough mental map of where the (limited) coverage is in the western half. When you get Amazonian rounds, this can prevent you from wildly plonking hundreds of kilometres away from the nearest road.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most coverage is in the eastern half, with very little in the Amazon. Learn where western roads are so you do not guess hundreds of km from the nearest road.

clues.title: Phone numbers: two-digit area codes
text: **Area codes** are common to see in Brazil. They are often notated using parentheses, or at minimum as two separate numbers. Phone numbers are sometimes without area codes, and without them will be 8 numbers long for landline and 9 for mobile.

The pattern for each of the states is very learnable and useful. The area codes are grouped by first digit, so even just learning those can already help a lot. Notably, area codes ending in 1 will always be around major cities and state capitals.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Area codes in brackets or as a separate number. Without them, landlines have 8 digits and mobiles 9. Codes are grouped by first digit, and codes ending in 1 are around big cities and capitals.

clues.title: Route marker: two-letter state codes
text: Each Brazilian state has a **two-letter acronym**. These show up most prominently in the numbers of state roads (found on kilometre markers). They can also be found in other contexts however.

The state acronyms show up when you zoom out a little bit on Google maps, which is also possible in the minimap while in-game. However, for quick and or competitive games, it can be very useful to learn them by heart anyway, as this can help a lot with eliminating scanning time.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Each state has a two-letter code (SP, BA...), shown mainly in state road numbers on kilometre markers. It also shows on the map when you zoom out.

clues.title: Sign: postcodes on street signs
text: **Postcodes (CEP) **are seen frequently on [street signs](https://maps.app.goo.gl/wKc1PEDRwyae19DW8) in Brazil (though sometimes hard to read). The first two numbers will depict an area, a state or multiple states. The numbers go anti-clockwise from São Paulo, ending in Rio Grande do Sul.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Postcodes (CEP) on street signs: the first two digits point to a state or several states, numbered anti-clockwise from São Paulo to Rio Grande do Sul.

clues.title: Landscape: highest mountains near the south-east
text: Shown here is an **elevation map** of Brazil. It can help to have a rough mental map of where you can find mountains, and which regions are more flat. The highest mountains are generally found near the southeastern coast.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Elevation map: the highest mountains are near the south-east coast. Learn which regions are flat.

clues.title: Landscape: dry soil, shrubs and succulents
text: Northeastern Brazil can be identified by its **dry soil, shrubs and succulents** (the [Caatinga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caatinga) landscape). In rainy season coverage, the shrubs are still recognisable, but can be deceptively green.

images.caption: Dry thorny scrub beside a paved road under a blue sky

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Northeast has dry soil, shrubs and succulents (the Caatinga). In rainy-season coverage the shrubs can look deceptively green.

clues.title: Landscape: dense rainforest
text: The **Amazon** is a dense rainforest that comprises 40% of Brazil’s total area. Not many roads are within it, but those that are, mostly go through either biodiverse forest or grassy hills with sparse trees.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: The Amazon is dense rainforest covering 40% of the country. The few roads go through rich forest or grassy hills with few trees.

clues.title: Landscape: small grass hills, road rides over them
text: Acre has a unique landscape of **small grass hills** and sparsely growing trees. The roads often do not cut around the hills like in most of Brazil, but ride the hills instead. A similar landscape can also be seen near Maraba in the state of Pará.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Acre: small grassy hills with few trees, and roads that go over the hills instead of around them. A similar landscape exists near Marabá, Pará.

clues.title: Landscape: open grass plains, big distant mountains
text: Rural locations in Roraima are mostly open **grassy plains with large, distant mountains** in the background. Occasionally, you are on roads within the mountains. Furthermore, the grass in Roraima is distinctly thin, and grows in bunches.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Roraima: open grassy plains with large distant mountains behind, and thin grass growing in bunches. Sometimes the road goes through the mountains.

clues.title: Landscape: lush green fields, hilly or flat
text: The landscape in Rio Grande do Sul can be hilly or flat with lush, green fields. Southern areas can have some resemblance to Uruguay.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Rio Grande do Sul: lush green fields, hilly or flat. The south can look like Uruguay.

differs.how: Southern areas look similar to Uruguay

clues.title: Landscape: rolling grassy hills
text: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo often have **rolling grassy hills**.
clues.region: Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro, Espírito Santo

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Rolling grassy hills are common in Minas Gerais, Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo.

clues.title: Landscape: big mountains with exposed rock
text: Espírito Santo, and the surrounding areas, often have large mountains with **exposed rock**.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Large mountains with bare rock in Espírito Santo and the areas around it.

clues.title: Plants: Paraná pine with horizontal branches
text: These distinct trees, called **Paraná pines**, have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the end. They grow mainly in the southern Brazilian states of Paraná, Santa Catarina, and Rio Grande do Sul.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Paraná pines have long horizontal branches with leaves only at the tips. They grow mainly in Paraná, Santa Catarina and Rio Grande do Sul.

clues.title: Plants: coconut palms
text: Coconut palm trees have long leaves, **can grow very tall, and have thin trunks**. They are common across the north eastern states and sometimes further west or south along the coast.
NOTE: Coconut palms grow across the world and are not unique to Brazil.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Tall coconut palms with long leaves and thin trunks, common in the Northeast states and sometimes further west or south along the coast. They grow worldwide.

clues.title: Plants: carnaúba palms
text: Carnaúba palms have short but strong **fan-like leaves**, and a trunk that is smooth at the top and spiked at the bottom. They are commonly seen in Ceará, Piauí, and Rio Grande de Norte, but are also around the town of Xique Xique in Bahia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Carnaúba palms: short strong fan leaves, trunk smooth at the top and spiky at the bottom. Common in Ceará, Piauí and Rio Grande do Norte, and around Xique-Xique in Bahia.

clues.title: Plants: babassu palms
text: Babassu palms have long, robust leaves comprised of many leaflets. Trunk length can vary from short to tall. They are found throughout the Amazon, or more rarely, down the east coast.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Babassu palms: long robust leaves of many leaflets, trunk short or tall. Found throughout the Amazon, more rarely down the east coast.

clues.title: Plants: açaí palms
text: Açai palms produce fruits that are popular globally. Most of these palms are found near Belem, but can be seen across the Amazon. They are distinct in the way the **leaflets droop downward** along with their unusually thin trunks.

NOTE: Most açai palms are found in the Amazon. However, some [visually similar açai subspecies](https://maps.app.goo.gl/qiyQrPPTzgZqcnz88) can rarely occur along the east coast from Santa Catarina all the way to Bahia.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Açaí palms have drooping leaflets and unusually thin trunks. Most are near Belém, spread across the Amazon. Similar subspecies rarely grow along the coast from Santa Catarina to Bahia.

clues.title: Plants: moriche palms
text: Moriche palms have leaves with a **rounded fan shape**, and often the bottom leaves can be seen **dead and drooping down**. They are most common in Roraima, Amazonas, Tocantins, Goias, and the Amazonian states, but random clusters can be found quite far away from this region.
NOTE: These palms can additionally be found very commonly in the [Amazonian parts of Colombia and Peru](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/7/71/Distribution_of_Mauritia_flexuosa.png).

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Moriche palms: rounded fan leaves, dead bottom leaves hanging down. Most common in Roraima, Amazonas, Tocantins and Goiás, with random clusters further away. Also very common in Amazonian Colombia and Peru.

clues.title: Plants: macaw palms
text: Macaw palms have **thin leaves** compared to other palms, and often have a visible** spear** **shaped** top. They are very common around Mato Grosso do Sul, northern Tocantins, and around Belo Horizonte, but can be seen much further out sometimes. These palms should be used with caution, and single trees are much less of an indicator than multiple trees.
NOTE: [Queen palms](https://maps.app.goo.gl/FqKSDoQwW74P3ES89) can look similar sometimes, but there are less leaves and it looks less dense.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Macaw palms: thin leaves, often a spear-shaped top. Very common around Mato Grosso do Sul, northern Tocantins and Belo Horizonte. One tree is a weak clue, several are better. Queen palms look similar but have fewer, less dense leaves.

clues.title: Plants: long-stemmed leafy plant in the north-east
text: This species of plant, with **long stems** and many leaves growing up, are very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, and Paraíba. In the dry season, you can still make out the distinct long stems without leaves.
clues.region: Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte, Paraíba

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A plant with long stems and upward leaves, very common in Ceará, Rio Grande do Norte and Paraíba. In the dry season the long bare stems still show.

clues.title: Plants: very tall grass in the centre
text: **Very tall grass** can be often seen in the centre of the country, most notably in the Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia, and Minas Gerais states.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Very tall grass is often seen in the centre, most of all in Tocantins, Goiás, Bahia and Minas Gerais.

clues.title: Plants: eucalyptus plantations
text: **Eucalyptus Grandis**, when fully grown, is a very tall tree with plantations all over Brazil. You can find them in both large and very small plantations., as well as randomly growing anywhere. You can see them all over the south, but there are some large plantations in Amapá too.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Very tall eucalyptus in big or small plantations or growing anywhere. Seen all over the south, with some large plantations in Amapá too.

clues.title: Plants: sugarcane
text: **Sugarcane plantations** are by far most common in the state of São Paulo, and are common in Paraná, Mato Grosso do Sul, and in the coastal north eastern states.
clues.region: São Paulo, Paraná, Mato Grosso do Sul

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Sugarcane is by far most common in São Paulo, and common in Paraná, Mato Grosso do Sul and the coastal Northeast states.

clues.title: Plants: soybeans
text: **Soybeans** appear as small, leafy soil grown plants. They are most commonly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná, and Goiás.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Small leafy soybean plants, mostly grown in Mato Grosso, Paraná and Goiás.

clues.title: Plants: coffee
text: **Coffee beans** are by far the most common in Minas Gerais, but also can be found in Espírito Santo and northeastern São Paulo.
clues.region: Minas Gerais, Espírito Santo, São Paulo

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Coffee is by far most common in Minas Gerais, but also in Espírito Santo and north-eastern São Paulo.

clues.title: Pole: round concrete poles in the south
text: Alongside ladder poles, **round poles** can often be found across the south of Brazil, especially São Paulo. These poles are cylindrical and made of concrete.

NOTE: This map and the following wooden pole map was created using statistical analysis of semi-urban and rural locations. 434 locations of 3 poles per location were used across 16 states that were thought to have mixed poles. Regardless of the state, the centre of large cities will often have round poles.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Besides ladder poles, round concrete poles are common in the south, especially São Paulo. Big-city centres often have round poles anywhere.

clues.title: Pole: wooden poles in some states
text: Some states also use **wooden poles**. They are most commonly seen in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas, and Rio de Janeiro.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Wooden poles are most common in Rio Grande do Sul, Roraima, Amazonas and Rio de Janeiro.

clues.title: Pole: support bars linking crossbar to pole
text: Brazil often uses **supports **on its electricity poles that connect the crossbar to the stem of the pole. The frequency of pole supports varies greatly state-to-state. It is notably rare in the northeast.
NOTE: This tip only works for poles that have a crossbar.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Supports link the crossbar to the pole. How often depends on the state, and they are notably rare in the Northeast. Only works on poles with a crossbar.

clues.title: Pole: single support bar
text: Poles with a **single support **are most commonly found in the states of Tocantins, Santa Catarina, and Minas Gerais.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Poles with a single support are most common in Tocantins, Santa Catarina and Minas Gerais.

clues.title: Pole: long yellow ID, black code with a letter
text: Markings on poles are used by the electricity companies to identify them. This pole ID is **long**, **yellow** **pole paint **with a black code. The ones that start with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Long yellow pole paint with a black code. Codes starting with a letter are found in Bahia and Pernambuco.

clues.title: Pole: long yellow paint ID starting with a number
text: Similar to the Bahia and Pernambuco poles, Goiás poles also use **long, yellow pole paint **with a black paint code, but it always starts with a number. They also have a rarer yellow on black pole ID, which can be either paint or a plate.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Goiás: long yellow pole paint with a black code that always starts with a number. A rarer yellow-on-black ID, paint or plate, also exists there.

clues.title: Pole: small yellow or orange plate on the pole
text: This **small yellow or orange plate** attached onto the pole by thin metal or zip tie is found in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. This ID is usually much higher up the pole in Pernambuco than in Rio Grande do Norte.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A small yellow or orange plate fixed by thin metal or a zip tie, in Rio Grande do Norte and Pernambuco. It sits much higher on the pole in Pernambuco.

clues.title: Pole: black paint with yellow or white text
text: Pole IDs in Paraná are usually made up of **black paint** and yellow or white painted text.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Paraná, pole IDs are black paint with yellow or white text.

clues.title: Pole: small beige plate built into the pole
text: Most poles in Maranhão have a **small beige plate with numbers** built into the surface of the pole. This pole ID can be found in Pará and Piauí more rarely.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Most poles in Maranhão have a small beige numbered plate built into the pole. Rarer in Pará and Piauí.

clues.title: Pole: street name painted on junction poles
text: Utility poles in Paraná on intersections are sometimes **painted with the street name**. This can sometimes extend to Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul if there are ladder poles in the city.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: In Paraná, utility poles at junctions are sometimes painted with the street name. Sometimes also in Santa Catarina or Rio Grande do Sul where ladder poles exist.

clues.title: Pole: lopsided crossbar with support to its middle
text: This poletop, consisting of an **asymmetrical crossbar** and a **support** reaching to the middle of the longer** **part of the crossbar, is the most common poletop in the state of São Paulo. It can also be frequently seen in the states of Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A lopsided crossbar with a support reaching the middle of the longer arm. Most common in São Paulo; frequent in Rio Grande do Sul, Rio de Janeiro and Mato Grosso do Sul.

clues.title: Pole: lopsided crossbar with no supports
text: This **asymmetrical** **crossbar** with **no supports** is exclusive to Ceara and Rondonia.
NOTE: While the crossbar in Ceara is usually made of concrete, the [Rondonian variation](https://maps.app.goo.gl/nXUtLu6sWXvN4zfF8) features a metal crossbar, and is far less common.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A lopsided crossbar with no supports, only in Ceará and Rondônia. Usually concrete in Ceará; Rondônia has a rarer metal version.

clues.title: Pole: zigzag top bar on a flat crossbar
text: This pole configuration, featuring a zigzag-shaped top bar resting atop a flat crossbar, is exclusive to Ceara and Roraima. The pole is usually much larger than a regular electricity pole.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: A zigzag top bar on a flat crossbar, only in Ceará and Roraima. The pole is usually much bigger than normal.

clues.title: Pole: smooth cone on top (pencil pole)
text: Poles that have a smooth cone on top, often called a **pencil pole**,** **are common in the state of Rio de Janeiro and rarely in Brasília and Manaus.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Poles with a smooth cone on top like a pencil: common in Rio de Janeiro, rare in Brasília and Manaus.

clues.title: Pole: Γ-shaped with electricity boxes at the end
text: **Gamma-shaped ("Γ")** poles containing **electricity boxes** at the end of the bar are most commonly seen in the state of Rio de Janeiro and in the cities of Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió.
NOTE: A variation with a [shorter bar](https://maps.app.goo.gl/AQ9y7AkQfqjh7KjV9) is exclusive to Belém.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Γ-shaped poles with electricity boxes at the end, most common in Rio de Janeiro and the cities Belém, Salvador, Fortaleza and Maceió. A shorter-bar version is only in Belém.

clues.title: Pole: electricity counters attached to poles
text: You may frequently see** electricity counters** attached to the poles in Cuiabá, Macapá and large cities in the state of Pará.
NOTE: The electricity counter may consist of one or [several ](https://maps.app.goo.gl/cHRjDx6cB5YRJZHi7)compartments.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Electricity counters attached to poles are frequent in Cuiabá, Macapá and big cities in Pará. They can have one or several compartments.

clues.title: Pole: top insulator plus alternating side ones
text: Poles that have one insulator on top and **alternating** horizontal insulators can be found in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. It is also very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: One insulator on top and horizontal ones alternating below, in Mato Grosso and southern Acre. Very rare in Rio Grande do Sul.

clues.title: Insulator: brown mushroom-shaped
text: Insulators that resemble **brown mushrooms** are only found in Pernambuco.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Brown mushroom-shaped insulators are only found in Pernambuco.

clues.title: Insulator: white mushroom-shaped
text: Insulators that resemble **white mushrooms** are found in Bahia and rarely Brasília.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: White mushroom-shaped insulators are found in Bahia and rarely in Brasília.

clues.title: Insulator: transparent
text: **Transparent** insulators are mostly in Alagoas in the northeast, and Santa Catarina in the south. They can be seen rarely in Sergipe, Ceará, and Brasília.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Transparent insulators are mostly in Alagoas and Santa Catarina, and rarely in Sergipe, Ceará and Brasília.

clues.title: Insulator: spool-of-thread shape
text: These insulators have a shape resembling a **spool of thread**. They are found mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.

credit.licence: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0

clues.summary: Spool-of-thread insulators are mostly in Rio de Janeiro and Espírito Santo, and have been seen in Ceará.

clues.title: Insulator: long and thin
text: Insulators in Ceará can sometimes be uniquely **long and thin**. They are in Goiás too, but are rare.

text: **Long grey insulators**, not including when they are horizontal, are most commonly found in Pará, Mato Grosso, Tocantins, Bahia, Mato Grosso do Sul, Paraná and Santa Catarina.

clues.title: Plants: queen palms
text: **Queen palms** have leaf stems that point upwards on the trunk and then "bow down" again to the ground due to gravity. They are native to South America. In Brazil, they are mainly found along the **coast** between Rio de Janeiro and Porto Alegre.
Outside of South America, they're also found in Florida and East Coast Queensland.

clues.title: Plants: Paraguay palm (not macaw palm)
text: This palm is commonly mistaken to be a Macaw Palm (Acrocomia Aculeata). The key difference is that the trunk of the "Paraguay Palm" is often smoother and less irregular. The crown can also give some hints although it's difficult to catch the differences
Macaw Palm: More open and irregular, with leaves spreading in different directions.
"Paraguay Palm": Denser and more compact, sometimes looking neater and rounder.
The distribution is also a bit different, as this palm usually is closer to Paraguay than the Macaw Palm which stretches further.

images.caption: Crown of a Paraguay palm circled in red on top of a tall slim trunk

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Often mistaken for macaw palm, but the trunk is smoother and the crown denser and rounder. It occurs closer to Paraguay than the macaw palm does.

clues.title: Plants: juçara palm (not açaí)
text: Closely related to the Açaí palm, they are really hard to distinguish apart from each other. However, the Açaí palm grows mostly in the northern flat regions of Brazil, while the Juçara grows in the mountainous south-east regions of Brazil anywhere from Espirito Santo down to Rio Grande do Sul.
Here some tips for differences:
The leaves of Jucara Palms are thinner
Jucara Palms have more space, they don't like growing close to each other.

credit.licence: Learnable Meta; notes partly from Plonk It (CC BY-NC-SA 4.0)

clues.summary: Closely related to açaí. Açaí grows in the flat north; juçara in the mountainous south-east, from Espírito Santo down to Rio Grande do Sul. Juçara has thinner leaves and grows with more space between plants.
